anatomy.title: Case Map
anatomy.subtitle: Transnational criminal prosecution: how a state deploys legal instruments beyond the limits of its own jurisdiction.
anatomy.text:
Transnational repression rarely begins with violence — it begins with paperwork. Arbitration, three court instances up to the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, all confirmed: the transaction was lawful. Then the same facts became the basis of a criminal charge. This is the classic mechanics of politically motivated prosecution: a legal system used not to establish truth, but to achieve a predetermined outcome.

In Serbia, the extradition request was treated primarily as a procedural document rather than an independent review of the legitimacy of the prosecution. The case passed through three court instances and now awaits the signature of the Minister of Justice.

Within Russia, not a single authority examined the defence's arguments on the merits. The Moscow Regional Prosecutor's Office, the Prosecutor General, the Moscow City Court: referrals, registrations, form letters. Not procedural failures — a systemic and documented denial of justice.

When domestic mechanisms are closed, international ones remain: the Interpol CCF to challenge the Red Notice, UNHCR to assess the risks of persecution, Ukrainian authorities in connection with specific circumstances of the case. All three have been engaged.
anatomy.manifesto: To recognise this extradition request as lawful is to establish a precedent: a state may use the extradition mechanism to pursue a person whose conduct its own courts have already found to be lawful. This is not an anomaly of a single case — it is a structural vulnerability affecting anyone who has left a country with a functioning prosecutorial apparatus and the political will to use it.

legal.title: Legal dissonance
legal.text: The Moscow Regional Arbitration Court, the appellate and cassation courts, and the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation all confirmed the lawfulness of the transaction in case No. A41-20164/2022. A criminal case opened concurrently characterises the same facts as fraud. The investigative record contains the defence's position on fair market value — and this is subsequently interpreted as evidence of intent to understate the price. Two mutually exclusive conclusions about the same fact, issued by institutions of the same state, are not a procedural inconsistency. They are a symptom of instrumentalised prosecution.
legal.question: How can demanding a fair market price serve as proof of intent to conceal it?

international.title: International track
international.text: Transnational repression is the practice by which a state pursues a person beyond its territory through available legal and extra-legal mechanisms: international wanted notices through Interpol, extradition requests, and diplomatic pressure. All three forms are present in this case: an Interpol Red Notice (challenged before the CCF), a formal extradition request to Serbia, and submissions to UNHCR. Each of these mechanisms provides for independent review of the legitimacy of the prosecution — and that review is the subject of this archive.

actors.title: Participants
actors.text: The criminal case was opened by the investigative authorities of the Moscow Region. The extradition request was transmitted by the Prosecutor General of the Russian Federation. The request was ruled upon by Serbian courts across three instances; the final instrument awaits the signature of the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Serbia. In parallel: the Interpol CCF is examining the challenge to the Red Notice; UNHCR is processing the asylum application; the Constitutional Court of Serbia is considering a constitutional complaint. All participants, the dates of their authority, and the acts they issued are documented without editorial commentary.

archive.text: Primary sources without editorial revision or authorial interpretation. The archive is structured around four sections, each corresponding to a distinct legal dimension of the case. Documents are published in the form in which they were received from the competent authorities:

flagrant.title: Flagrant denial of justice
flagrant.text: Under ECHR standards, a 'flagrant denial of justice' is a violation of the right to a fair trial so severe that it constitutes an independent ground for refusing extradition — regardless of the merits of the underlying charge. In this case: more than 8 submissions to the Moscow Regional Prosecutor's Office — all referred elsewhere or rejected without examination on the merits; 5 submissions to the Prosecutor General — the same result; a complaint to the Moscow City Court — refused as inadmissible. Not one authority issued a decision containing any substantive assessment of the defence's arguments.

news.title: EU Delegation Response: Meeting Scheduled
news.desc: The European Union Delegation in Belgrade has responded to the defence's submission. A working meeting has been scheduled to discuss extradition risks and human rights compliance.

news.title: GPO Refusal to Review Falsification Claims
news.desc: Deputy Prosecutor General Prokopenko rejected the complaint against investigator Salikov, ignoring documented evidence of forgery in the inspection records.

news.title: RFE/RL Feature: 'Six Months Without a Minister's Signature'
news.desc: An in-depth report on the Lagovsky case, highlighting the legal vacuum, the family's lack of health insurance, and the wait for the Justice Minister's political decision.

news.title: Submission to UNHCR
news.desc: The defence submitted a comprehensive evidence package to the UN refugee agency in Serbia, documenting risks of persecution on political and ethnic grounds.

news.title: Final Asylum Refusal
news.desc: The Commission upheld the refusal, declining to examine arguments regarding family life (Art. 8 ECHR). An appeal has been lodged with the Administrative Court.
